Cape Town Fire Season 2017

By: Michael Duffett | Production

Proposal


Show:

Unique Selling Point:
It's back with a vengeance. Deadly fires springing up all over the Cape Peninsula - from Somerset West to Paarl, Simons Town and the City Bowl. We meet and hear gut wrenching stories from people who have lost everything or had to to flee for their lives. Facebook is full of praise for the firemen on the ground - but the question remains - why so many fires? Increasingly the perception is that it is arson. The people we will be interviewing are as follows:
1. Fire Chief
2. JP Smith
3. Three victims
4. Justin Sullivan - a young man who specialises in capturing the fires on camera and has followed each fire in the Cape.

We will try and also get to speak to fireman and get on a firetruck and go to a fire and speak to people as they are fighting the fire.

Press Release:


Cape Fires
Cape Town firefighters are responding to a staggering 75 fires per day. The flames have wreaked havoc, leaving many no choice but to escape with only the clothes on their backs. The spate of fires has led many to question whether some were started deliberately. Carte Blanche meets the heroes saving lives and the residents who’ve lost everything.


Script:


Hellish scenes as cape fires tore through land and property, destroying several historic buildings in its wake, forcing residents and animals to flee, helicopters swooping in to douse the angry flames and exhausted firefighters going beyond the call of duty to limit the damage.

JP Smith: Our worst day so far 126 fires, so where the firefighters say on the front page of the newspaper that they are feeling overworked, they are feeling over worked. Its hard during the season when you go from one massive conflagration to the next.

Link: There is a fire season every year in the western cape but this year due to one of the worst droughts in 100 years and a roaring south Easter, it started much earlier than normal.

Powerful images drawing attention to the fires are being posted onto social media by cape town photographer and videographer Justin Sullivan

Justin Sullivan: There’s this chaotic destruction going on around me and I'm trying to stay calm and see if I can get the best angles to portray what is happening in the most raw reality you know.

John: Is it realistic to assume that with the numbers of fires, that they are all starting naturally?
JP Smith: No sir, no there is definitely a lot of suspicious stuff. Many of these fires are starting under circumstances that are just strange. They are starting in places where there is no human habitation.

We heard from an Inspector from the Helderberg Animal Welfare Society who, while attending a fire in grabouw earlier this week, noticed children lighting matches nearby.

Robin Lansdale: Just noting looking up at grabouw lodge and we just noticed all these little youngsters walking past there and literally actually starting the fire just outside grabouw lodge and then making a duck up the sand dunes over the mountain.

JP Smith: Some of it is just kids being naughty. We have interviewed children caught in the act who said they light the fire because it brings the helicopters.


On social media there has been much talk about unverified voice recordings which have been posted suggesting arson. This is an example:
(In Afrikaans) We watched them through the binoculars. We saw them. We saw how they set places alight.

There is also controversy over a social media posting by Lindsay Maasdorp from the organization Black First Land First. It reads black god needs servants in CT: wind + matches +white owned farms. We asked him about the tweet and Facebook post.

Lindsay Maasdorp: It was just basically an observation of fire and wind and thankful to god for moments of intervention in black oppression.
John: In a nutshell, are you asking people to commit arson, to start fires? Or are you talking more sort of hypothetically?
Lindsay Maasdorp: I have never asked anyone to start fires and I’m not asking anyone to start fires. If people decide that their lived oppression makes them to respond in a way where fires begin. That is for them to decide. Not for me to decide.


According to JP Smith, the city is considering laying charges of hate speech.

Jp Smith: He may well be inspiring other people who are somewhat unhinged to go and do such actions and those actions may cause the death of a person of any color and any death of a human being or even death of animals to us is a seriously egregious matter, on top of the economic damages.

Whatever the cause, it has been a busy month for Sullivan who underwent a fire fighting course to become imbedded with the city’s fire services. He was on the scene when the first major fire of the new year broke out in Somerset west on the 3rd of January. It lasted for several days, destroying properties and vast tracks of land.

A week later he was on hand in Simons town and its surrounding when another huge fire ignited causing residents to evacuate. Next up was Paarl, about 45 minutes outside Cape Town.

LINK: This valley has an extraordinary history. This building for example has been here since 1692 but in the space of a week, this farm and others like it, were engulfed by flames.

On the 9th of January a fire broke out on Du Toits Kloof mountains above the town Fuelled by gusting winds, the fire raced towards the farms below, catching many residents off guard. The Drakenstein Farm watch fire fighting group was in the thick of things.

Daan van Leeuwen Boomkamp: They were very brave. They went first in with normal cars to go and wake everybody because that fire spreads with 20, 30km an hour so you can’t outrun it even. So we have to kick in doors, get people out of their beds and there is no time for discussion, sometimes even we literally drag them out and then look there, then they see the fire and then they only realize what’s going on.

Frightened residents were evacuated. Farm animals and pets were taken to safety as part of the rescue operation.

On the august Kleinbosch Farm, the first Afrikaans school in south Africa built in the 1880's was completely destroyed. As was the wine farm and homestead of Dorothee Kirchner. She was awoken during the night by frantic barking.

Dorothee Kirchner: I could see there were sparks coming through the air and were settling in the thatch roof and started the fire.
John: That must have been terrifying?
Dorothee: It was very terrifying. I never saw something like this. It was like a very bad movie.
John: how did you respond in that moment? What was your first instinct?
Dorothee: I only had a sleeping shirt on so I grabbed the jeans and went downstairs, grabbed my dogs and car key and left the house and I think at this point I just wanted to save my life and the ones of my dogs obviously.


When she returned the net morning, there was nothing left. On a neighboring farm Konstantin Fedetov was assisting residents at a shelter and helping to douse a nearby fire.

Konstantin Fedetov: And 1 hour later, the fire started and broke over here and then its just the ashes and everything and while we were fighting the fire down there, the roof caught on fire.

All he could do was look on helplessly as his historic home was engulfed and reduced to ruins.

Antony Goosen who had worked on this farm for 20 years was heart broken.

Anthony Goosen: (in Afrikaans) There are no words to say. It's almost as if my whole life is going. For me...to grow up in a place and see it burn down is heartbreaking.

Next, the cape town city bowl was hit on the 17th January.

LINK: this part of cape town deals with fires almost on an annual basis and this year was no different. But it as also meant that they have had to pull together as a community.

The fire rushed down from Devils Peak and many residents grabbed everything and fled. One of those who evacuated was Josette Maeyer. Later that night when she and her husband returned, the fire flared up again.

Josette Maeyer: That’s when we saw the fire appearing behind these houses here and we were watching very carefully. The next minute, the fire hit a palm tree at the back of one of these houses.

Her husband photographer that tree exploding which sent embers every where, causing several homes to be damaged. Devils peak resident, Melanie Verwoerd says fires are so common in the area, the communities WhatsApp group has become a crucial means of communication. She has nothing but praise for the firefighters.

Melanie: It is absolutely extraordinary how fearless they go into these fires. Last year when the fire was so thick, we could not in our road, we could not even see each other, the smoke was so thick. You can’t breathe. These guys walk into those flames.
Josette: They are amazing. They are our heroes.

Sullivan who is often on the font line agrees that they are utterly committed.

Justin: I think the guys work extremely hard you know. A lot of them sometimes work a 24 hour shifts. They really put their bodies on the line, but they also very well trained so they know where their limit is and often they need to step away from the smoke to get some fresh air before they go back in. If they are too tired, the crew leaders are brilliant. They always say listen you've had too much, lets move yourself of the line.

Social media is filled with praise for these exhausted fire fighters. Something that please fire chief Ian Schnetler.

Ian: And when the acknowledgment comes from the public and particularly management, that does lift and it does boost the morale at the end of the day and and you know at the end of the 24 hour shift when they might just have to work another hour, that just gives them the boost to work that extra hour and do the job and get it done.

The collateral damage of course is the wild life, often caught up in the fires. Here at the SPCA several different welfare organizations meet to plan future rescue operations because the fire season is far from over. Scores of animals have been affected, with many rescues, such as these two injured baby birds. And scenes of confused baboons are tugging at the heartstrings of animal lovers across south Africa.

According to Minette Pieterse the injured baboons are being monitored by vets and welfare authorities.

Minette: So they have decided to leave them there, check on them daily and monitor them then. If they see something is happening and they going downhill, then they will remove them as soon as possible but for now it is just monitoring in the wild.

Back in Paarl it’s a time to pick up the pieces.

Konstantin: Rebuild. Definitely. Bigger, better, stronger and go on.
John: You are determined to move on?
Konstantin: Yah absolutely.

Kirchner is just as resolute.

Dorothee: Yah we wont let this get us down. We will build up again, nobody will lose their job, that is for sure.


But Sullivan, whose mission it is to raise awareness through his images which he provides free of charge, knows that more devastation is on the horizon for the fire season has just begun in the cape.

Justin: It is very busy and its only the start of the season. February I think is usually the month when it burns the most.
John: Yes, so you likely to take a lot more photos?
Justin: I think so, yes...

Social media is filled with praise for these exhausted fire fighters. Something that please fire chief Ian Schnetler. Ian: And when the acknowledgment comes from the public and particularly management, that does lift and it does boost the morale at the end of the day and and you know at the end of the 24 hour shift when they might just have to work another hour, that just gives them the boost to work that extra hour and do the job and get it done. The collateral damage of course is the wild life, often caught up in the fires. Here at the SPCA several different welfare organizations meet to plan future rescue operations because the fire season is far from over. Scores of animals have been affected, with many rescues, such as these two injured baby birds. And scenes of confused baboons are tugging at the heartstrings of animal lovers across south Africa. According to Minette Pieterse the injured baboons are being monitored by vets and welfare authorities. Minette: So they have decided to leave them there, check on them daily and monitor them then. If they see something is happening and they going downhill, then they will remove them as soon as possible but for now it is just monitoring in the wild. Back in Paarl it’s a time to pick up the pieces. Konstantin: Rebuild. Definitely. Bigger, better, stronger and go on. John: You are determined to move on? Konstantin: Yah absolutely. Kirchner is just as resolute. Dorothee: Yah we wont let this get us down. We will build up again, nobody will lose their job, that is for sure. But Sullivan, whose mission it is to raise awareness through his images which he provides free of charge, knows that more devastation is on the horizon for the fire season has just begun in the cape. Justin: It is very busy and its only the start of the season. February I think is usually the month when it burns the most. John: Yes, so you likely to take a lot more photos? metadata.Unique Selling Point: It's back with a vengeance. Deadly fires springing up all over the Cape Peninsula - from Somerset West to Paarl, Simons Town and the City Bowl. We meet and hear gut wrenching stories from people who have lost everything or had to to flee for their lives. Facebook is full of praise for the firemen on the ground - but the question remains - why so many fires? Increasingly the perception is that it is arson. The people we will be interviewing are as follows: 1. Fire Chief 2. JP Smith 3. Three victims 4. Justin Sullivan - a young man who specialises in capturing the fires on camera and has followed each fire in the Cape. We will try and also get to speak to fireman and get on a firetruck and go to a fire and speak to people as they are fighting the fire.
